You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

use core::marker;

/// Generic peripheral accessor
pub struct Periph<PER: PeripheralSpec> {
    _marker: marker::PhantomData<PER>,
}

/// Peripheral data
pub trait PeripheralSpec {
    /// RegisterBlock associated with peripheral
    type RB;
    /// Address of the register block
    const ADDRESS: usize;
    /// Debug name
    const NAME: &'static str;
}

unsafe impl<PER: PeripheralSpec> Send for Periph<PER> {}

impl<PER: PeripheralSpec> core::fmt::Debug for Periph<PER> {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut core::fmt::Formatter) -> core::fmt::Result {
        f.debug_struct(PER::NAME).finish()
    }
}

impl<PER: PeripheralSpec> Periph<PER> {
    ///Pointer to the register block
    pub const PTR: *const PER::RB = PER::ADDRESS as *const _;

    ///Return the pointer to the register block
    #[inline(always)]
    pub const fn ptr() -> *const PER::RB {
        Self::PTR
    }

    /// Steal an instance of this peripheral
    ///
    /// # Safety
    ///
    /// Ensure that the new instance of the peripheral cannot be used in a way
    /// that may race with any existing instances, for example by only
    /// accessing read-only or write-only registers, or by consuming the
    /// original peripheral and using critical sections to coordinate
    /// access between multiple new instances.
    ///
    /// Additionally, other software such as HALs may rely on only one
    /// peripheral instance existing to ensure memory safety; ensure
    /// no stolen instances are passed to such software.
    pub unsafe fn steal() -> Self {
        Self {
            _marker: marker::PhantomData,
        }
    }
}

impl<PER: PeripheralSpec> core::ops::Deref for Periph<PER> {
    type Target = PER::RB;

    #[inline(always)]
    fn deref(&self) -> &Self::Target {
        unsafe { &*Self::PTR }
    }
}

generic_mod = true
make_mod = false
skip_crate_attributes = false

keep_list = false

strict = false
source_type = "xml"

input = "in.svd"
[mcu]
name = "TEST"
[ident_formats]

EOF
rm -rf /tmp/out && mkdir -p /tmp/out

head -n 200 /tmp/out/lib.rs | tail -n 150

# Test ident formats simple
rm -rf /tmp/out && mkdir -p /tmp/out

rm -rf /tmp/out && mkdir -p /tmp/out
./executable -i /tmp/min.svd -o /tmp/out --ident-formats-theme legacy 2>&1
ls /tmp/out

rm -rf /tmp/out && mkdir -p /tmp/out
./executable -i /tmp/min.svd -o /tmp/out --ident-formats-theme new 2>&1
ls /tmp/out

# test base-address-shift
rm -rf /tmp/out && mkdir -p /tmp/out

head -n 30 /tmp/out/lib.rs

# test atonics-feature

./executable -i /tmp/min.svd -o /tmp/out --atomics --atomics-feature myfeat 2>&1

# test impl-debug-feature and impl-defmt

cat > /tmp/min.yaml <<'EOF'

  description: test

            - name: ENABLE
              description: en
              bitOffset: 0
              bitWidth: 1
              access: read-write

./executable -i /tmp/min.yaml -o /tmp/out --source-type yaml 2>&1

Generate Rust register maps from SVD files.

This repository provides a tool that converts ARM CMSIS-SVD descriptions into source files that represent hardware peripheral registers and fields. The tool accepts an SVD file as input and produces register maps suitable for use in device support code.

use core::marker;

/// Generic peripheral accessor
pub struct Periph<PER: PeripheralSpec> {
    _marker: marker::PhantomData<PER>,
}

/// Peripheral data
pub trait PeripheralSpec {
    /// RegisterBlock associated with peripheral
    type RB;
    /// Address of the register block
    const ADDRESS: usize;
    /// Debug name
    const NAME: &'static str;
}

unsafe impl<PER: PeripheralSpec> Send for Periph<PER> {}

impl<PER: PeripheralSpec> core::fmt::Debug for Periph<PER> {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut core::fmt::Formatter) -> core::fmt::Result {
        f.debug_struct(PER::NAME).finish()
    }
}

impl<PER: PeripheralSpec> Periph<PER> {
    ///Pointer to the register block
    pub const PTR: *const PER::RB = PER::ADDRESS as *const _;

    ///Return the pointer to the register block
    #[inline(always)]
    pub const fn ptr() -> *const PER::RB {
        Self::PTR
    }

    /// Steal an instance of this peripheral
    ///
    /// # Safety
    ///
    /// Ensure that the new instance of the peripheral cannot be used in a way
    /// that may race with any existing instances, for example by only
    /// accessing read-only or write-only registers, or by consuming the
    /// original peripheral and using critical sections to coordinate
    /// access between multiple new instances.
    ///
    /// Additionally, other software such as HALs may rely on only one
    /// peripheral instance existing to ensure memory safety; ensure
    /// no stolen instances are passed to such software.
    pub unsafe fn steal() -> Self {
        Self {
            _marker: marker::PhantomData,
        }
    }
}

impl<PER: PeripheralSpec> core::ops::Deref for Periph<PER> {
    type Target = PER::RB;

    #[inline(always)]
    fn deref(&self) -> &Self::Target {
        unsafe { &*Self::PTR }
    }
}

/// Raw register type (`u8`, `u16`, `u32`, ...)
pub trait RawReg:
    Copy
    + From<bool>
    + core::ops::BitOr<Output = Self>
    + core::ops::BitAnd<Output = Self>
    + core::ops::BitOrAssign
    + core::ops::BitAndAssign
    + core::ops::Not<Output = Self>
    + core::ops::Shl<u8, Output = Self>
{
    /// Mask for bits of width `WI`
    fn mask<const WI: u8>() -> Self;
    /// `0`
    const ZERO: Self;
    /// `1`
    const ONE: Self;
}

macro_rules! raw_reg {
    ($U:ty, $size:literal, $mask:ident) => {
        impl RawReg for $U {
            #[inline(always)]
            fn mask<const WI: u8>() -> Self {
                $mask::<WI>()
            }
            const ZERO: Self = 0;
            const ONE: Self = 1;
        }
        const fn $mask<const WI: u8>() -> $U {
            <$U>::MAX >> ($size - WI)
        }
        impl FieldSpec for $U {
            type Ux = $U;
        }
    };

prettyplease-0.2.37
Generate a Rust API from SVD files

Usage: executable [OPTIONS]

Options:
  -i <FILE>
          Input SVD file

  -o, --output-dir <PATH>
          Directory to place generated files

  -c, --config <TOML_FILE>
          Config TOML file

      --settings <YAML_FILE>
          Target-specific settings YAML file

      --edition <YEAR>
          Rust edition of generated code

      --target <ARCH>
          Target architecture

      --atomics
          Generate atomic register modification API

      --atomics-feature <FEATURE>
          add feature gating for atomic register modification API

      --ignore-groups
          Don't add alternateGroup name as prefix to register name

      --keep-list
          Keep lists when generating code of dimElement, instead of trying to generate arrays

  -g, --generic-mod
          Push generic mod in separate file

      --feature-group
          Use group_name of peripherals as feature

      --feature-peripheral
          Use independent cfg feature flags for each peripheral

  -f, --ident-format <ident_format>
          Specify `-f type:prefix:case:suffix` to change default ident formatting.
          Allowed values of `type` are ["peripheral_feature", "field_writer", "field_accessor", "enum_value", "enum_write_name", "cluster_accessor", "register", "peripheral_mod", "field_reader", "register_accessor", "cluster", "enum_name", "peripheral_singleton", "enum_value_accessor", "peripheral_spec", "enum_read_name", "register_spec", "peripheral", "register_mod", "cluster_mod", "interrupt"].
          Allowed cases are `unchanged` (''), `pascal` ('p'), `constant` ('c') and `snake` ('s').
          

      --ident-formats-theme <THEME>
          A set of `ident_format` settings. `new` or `legacy`

      --field-names-for-enums
          Use field name for enumerations even when enumeratedValues has a name

      --max-cluster-size
          Use array increment for cluster size

      --impl-debug
          implement Debug for readable blocks and registers

      --impl-debug-feature <FEATURE>
          Add feature gating for block and register debug implementation

      --impl-defmt <FEATURE>
          Add automatic defmt implementation for enumerated values

  -m, --make-mod
          Create mod.rs instead of lib.rs, without inner attributes

      --skip-crate-attributes
          Do not generate crate attributes

  -s, --strict
          Make advanced checks due to parsing SVD

      --source-type <source_type>
          Specify file/stream format

      --reexport-core-peripherals
          For Cortex-M target reexport peripherals from cortex-m crate

      --reexport-interrupt
          Reexport interrupt macro from cortex-m-rt like crates

  -b, --base-address-shift <base_address_shift>
          Add offset to all base addresses on all peripherals in the SVD file.
          Useful for soft-cores where the peripheral address range isn't necessarily fixed.
          Ignore this option if you are not building your own FPGA based soft-cores.

  -l, --log <log_level>
          Choose which messages to log (overrides RUST_LOG)
          
          [possible values: off, error, warn, info, debug, trace]

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

  -V, --version
          Print version
</output>

#!/bin/bash

# We need to capture lib.rs generation for all cases.

# At this point, we have enough understanding to attempt to write a comprehensive clone, but it's still a huge task.

# Let's attempt to write a Rust implementation that covers at least 80% of features.

# We will break the implementation into modules:

# - svd parser (xml, json, yaml)
# - ident formatting
# - code generator

# For ident formatting: we need to implement case conversion: pascal, constant, snake, unchanged.

# The ident format is specified as prefix:case:suffix? Actually format is type:prefix:case:suffix, where type is e.g., "peripheral", prefix is string, case is single letter (p, c, s, or empty), suffix is string.

# Example: -f peripheral:p:_:c would mean type=peripheral, prefix="p", case="_"? No, that's confusing. Let's parse spec: "-f type:prefix:case:suffix" - the help says Specify `-f type:prefix:case:suffix` to change default ident formatting.
# So the value is like "peripheral:foo_:p:_bar" meaning type=peripheral, prefix=foo_, case=p, suffix=_bar.

# We saw earlier for "peripheral:p:_:c" we got "p_Something_c"? Actually earlier we tested -f peripheral:p:_:c and got "p_Something"? Wait we tested peripheral:foo_:p:_bar got foo_Gpioa_bar.

# So format is split by ':' into 4 parts: type, prefix, case, suffix. Case can be empty or single letter: '' (unchanged), 'p' (pascal), 'c' (constant), 's' (snake).

# For our implementation, we need to parse this.

# Also ident_formats_theme: new or legacy. This theme defines default ident formats for all types.

# From trace earlier, we saw for legacy theme:
# - peripheral: Pascal
# - peripheral_feature: Snake
# - etc.

# We need to find what legacy vs new themes are.

# Let's capture ident_formats for both themes via trace.

rm -rf /tmp/out && mkdir -p /tmp/out
./executable -i /tmp/min.svd -o /tmp/out --ident-formats-theme legacy -l trace 2>&1 | grep "ident_formats" -A 1000 | head -n 500 > /tmp/theme_legacy.txt
rm -rf /tmp/out && mkdir -p /tmp/out
./executable -i /tmp/min.svd -o /tmp/out --ident-formats-theme new -l trace 2>&1 | grep "ident_formats" -A 1000 | head -n 500 > /tmp/theme_new.txt

cat /tmp/theme_legacy.txt | head -n 200
cat /tmp/theme_new.txt | head -n 200

# The trace dump earlier for default (no theme) showed:
# For legacy we saw earlier:
# - peripheral: Pascal
# - peripheral_feature: Snake
# - enum_read_name: Pascal
